[PATH:empirical] Panel data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) or the UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS), stratified by income quintiles and household debt-to-income ratios — These longitudinal surveys track self-reported life satisfaction alongside detailed financial data across business cycles. Analyzing within-person changes during GDP contractions and expansions, and comparing subgroups with debt-to-income ratios above and below 40%, can directly test the asymmetric effect and the proposed amplification threshold.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country analysis using the World Values Survey or Gallup World Poll merged with macroeconomic data (GDP growth, household debt aggregates) from the IMF or OECD — A multi-country panel can examine whether the asymmetry in life satisfaction responses to GDP fluctuations is more pronounced in nations or time periods where lower-income households carry higher debt burdens. This would test the generalizability of the hypothesis beyond single-country contexts.

[PATH:theoretical] Behavioral economics literature on loss aversion and debt-induced stress (e.g., Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory, or recent work by De Neve et al. on wellbeing and economic shocks) — Reviewing and extending theoretical frameworks that predict asymmetric emotional responses to gains versus losses, especially under financial constraint, can provide mechanistic grounding. This would help assess whether the 40% debt-to-income threshold is a plausible inflection point for heightened loss sensitivity, and suggest additional moderators to test empirically.

[PATH:literature] Re-analysis of Kahneman and Deaton's (2010) or similar studies on emotional well-being and income, stratified by lower-income groups and linked to national GDP fluctuations. — Existing literature often finds that life satisfaction is more sensitive to income losses than gains (loss aversion), but this may differ by income level. A focused meta-analysis or replication using post-2000 data can confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of reference-dependent preferences (e.g., prospect theory) applied to subjective well-being, with calibration using microdata from developed economies. — Provides a framework to predict asymmetric responses and test whether lower-income groups exhibit steeper gains during expansions due to greater marginal utility of consumption, or sharper declines due to heightened loss aversion.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on local economic shocks (e.g., plant closures, natural experiments) measuring subsequent changes in social cohesion metrics in high-inequality vs. low-inequality areas — Such designs can isolate causal effects of negative economic shocks on trust and cohesion, testing if the response is asymmetric and moderated by inequality levels.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of loss aversion and social capital (e.g., behavioral economics frameworks incorporating prospect theory into community trust dynamics) — This would provide a mechanism explaining why trust might be more sensitive to losses (downturns) than gains (upturns) under inequality, and generate testable predictions for empirical validation.
